analysis.one_liner: Lets employees sue in court over rape, voiding forced-arbitration clauses for those claims.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past committee: it was referred to the Senate health and labor committee on March 24, 2015, drew no cosponsors, and received no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Many employers require workers to sign agreements sending any dispute to a private arbitrator instead of court. This bill would have made those agreements unenforceable for one specific kind of claim: a lawsuit arising out of rape. A worker who signed such an agreement could still go to court over that claim, before a judge and jury.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees (at companies with 15 or more workers) who have been forced to sign arbitration agreements and later bring a legal claim arising out of rape. Under current law, their employer can insist the claim be decided in private arbitration; this bill would have preserved their right to a public courtroom.

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that any employer-employee agreement to arbitrate 'shall not be enforceable with respect to any claim related to a tort arising out of rape,' so such a claim could proceed in court despite a signed arbitration clause.

The bill covers employers engaged in interstate commerce with 15 or more employees, essentially the same employer definition used in federal anti-discrimination law, and applies to most employees including those of state and local governments.
Congress's stated purpose is to 'preclude an employer from enforcing an agreement to arbitrate any claim related to a tort arising out of rape,' overriding contrary provisions in other laws.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with mandatory arbitration policies, which would lose the ability to keep rape-related claims out of court. That means public trials, jury exposure, and discovery for a category of claims they could previously channel to private arbitration. Arbitration providers would also forgo these cases.

drawbacks.text: The bill is extremely narrow: it covers only claims arising out of rape, leaving workers' other serious claims—assault, harassment, discrimination—still subject to forced arbitration, so it fixes a sliver of a larger problem while leaving the rest untouched.

Arbitration is not always worse for workers; it can be faster and cheaper than court, and employers could be expected to argue that carving out one category of claims creates inconsistency and litigation costs for all parties.

Because the bill was never debated, there was no hearing record on how often employers actually enforce arbitration agreements against rape-related claims, making the scope of the problem it addresses hard to verify from the legislative record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the narrow class of workers with a rape-related legal claim, the benefit is real: a public court hearing instead of a confidential arbitration the employer chose. The cost falls on employers, mainly in litigation exposure, and the honest criticism is design: by covering only rape claims, the bill acknowledges the problem with forced arbitration while solving almost none of it. A broader bill covering all harassment or assault claims would have helped far more workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate HELP committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, no other senator signed on, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator David Vitter introduced the bill on March 24, 2015 and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The committee took no further action on the bill; no markup, hearing, or floor vote appears in the action history for the remainder of the Congress.
No other senator cosponsored the bill at any point.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with mandatory arbitration agreements are better off: rape-related claims remain subject to forced arbitration, and no change in the law was made.

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and saw it referred to committee; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; it sat in committee from referral in March 2015 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None joined as cosponsors and none acted to bring the bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and was never debated or voted on, so no partisan split on the merits appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped employers' ability to force workers with rape-related claims into private arbitration, exposing them to jury trials and public court records. Their gain under the status quo is workers' loss of a public forum.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and law firms serving employers
industries.note: Rape-related employment claims would no longer be channelable to paid private arbitration, removing a small stream of business and the associated defense work.
